text: He moved his family in on June the fifteenth.
That night two bricks came through the front window.
His wife, Nannie, took to patrolling the house with a loaded pistol while the children slept.
One of those children was seven year old Lorraine Hansberry, who would grow up to write A Raisin in the Sun.
Years later she remembered that brick coming through the glass, missing her by inches, and she remembered her mother walking the rooms at night with the gun.
The Washington Park subdivision was covered by a covenant barring Black occupants, and within days the new neighbors filed suit to force the family out.
Hansberry did not move out.
He sued.
His lawyers found a crack in the paper.
The covenant was supposed to take effect only if the owners of ninety five percent of the frontage signed it, and in truth only about fifty four percent had.
The case reached the Supreme Court in 1940 as Hansberry versus Lee.
Hansberry won, but on narrow ground.
The Court did not say covenants were illegal.
It said this particular one had not been properly approved and could not bind him.
The wall had a gap in it.
The wall itself still stood.
It took eight more years to shake it.
The decisive case came from St.
Louis.
In 1945 a Black family named Shelley bought a home on Labadie Avenue, not knowing a covenant from 1911 forbade it.
A neighbor named Kraemer, who lived blocks away, sued to throw them out.
A nearly identical fight was unfolding in Detroit, where the McGhee family faced a covenant of its own.
